## What an analyst of the robustness study received {#what-an-analyst-received .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, usually taken from the abstract
- The **data**, or directions for fetching them
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; preregistration of the robustness study, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–5.
:::

::: notes
The SCORE robustness study gave a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each. I was one of those analysts, on a different paper from ours, and what arrived shapes how the results should be read. We received the whole published paper, not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, which if anything pulls an analyst towards the original answer. With it came the central claim in a single sentence, usually taken from the abstract, and the data or directions for fetching them, but no instruction on method beyond analysing the claim in any way that we could defend. [advance] Two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what they were finding. That isolation was part of the design, because it is what gives the spread of results at the end its meaning.
:::

## The two tasks of the robustness study {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages. Task one left the analysis entirely to the analyst, who then recorded one of four conclusions: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived, asking for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, with a short instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict, and task two whether they produce the same number, a question that can only be asked once everyone answers roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms, since each analyst reports the statistic that their model produces, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. The robustness study converted these statistics onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on one axis. A panel of peers also judged whether each analysis was appropriate for the claim, so the spread that the study reports is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted: that they estimate the same quantity, and that each conversion counts the units that carry the evidence. Much of what follows today concerns what happens when the first of these does not hold.
:::
